analysis.one_liner: Bans the manufacture, use, and sale of asbestos, with a phase-out for the chlorine industry.
analysis.headline: The bill has been introduced and sent to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, where no vote has been scheduled.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill amends the nation's main chemical safety law to prohibit making, processing, using, or selling commercial asbestos and products containing it, effective immediately when enacted. It defines the banned forms of asbestos to include eight mineral types, and it carves out two exceptions: chlorine plants that already use asbestos can keep using it until January 1, 2030, and the President can grant a temporary national-security exemption of up to three years, renewable once. Asbestos already installed in buildings and old products is left alone, and materials containing asbestos only as a trace impurity are excluded.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people, especially workers and their families who are exposed to asbestos on the job or through imported products. Asbestos fibers cause mesothelioma, lung cancer, and other diseases decades after exposure, and the bill would cut off new sources of exposure. First responders, firefighters, and people living near industrial users of asbestos would also gain from reduced emissions.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers, firefighters, and families exposed to asbestos

how_it_helps.text: The bill prohibits the manufacture, processing, use, and distribution in commerce of commercial asbestos and any mixture or article containing it, effective on the date of enactment [S2][S3].

The ban covers all eight recognized commercial asbestos minerals, including chrysotile, the only form still imported into the United States in significant quantities, used mainly by the chlor-alkali industry to make chlorine [S3].
Asbestos already installed in buildings is excluded so that the ban does not disrupt abatement or disposal, while materials with asbestos only as a trace impurity are also outside the ban [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The chlor-alkali industry, which uses asbestos to make chlorine, bears the cost of switching to non-asbestos technology by 2030. Importers and distributors of asbestos-containing products would lose their supply chains. The costs of the transition would ultimately show up in chlorine prices, which affect water treatment costs.

drawbacks.text: The bill gives chlor-alkali facilities in operation at enactment until January 1, 2030 to keep using asbestos, meaning known carcinogenic exposure continues for years in those plants and nearby communities [S3].
The President can grant national-security exemptions from the ban, renewable for up to six years, and can withhold publication of exemption details on national-security grounds [S2][S3].

The bill excludes asbestos present solely as an impurity and does not touch asbestos already installed in buildings, so it does not address the largest source of current exposure in the United States: legacy asbestos in older homes, schools, and workplaces [S3].

Environmental Protection Agency rules already finalized in 2024 banned ongoing uses of chrysotile asbestos with a similar chlor-alkali phase-out timeline, so the bill partly overlaps with existing regulation and its main effect would be writing that policy into statute where a future administration could more easily unwind a rule than a law.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The health benefit of ending new commercial uses of a known carcinogen is large and durable, and the bill leaves old asbestos in place rather than forcing expensive mass removal, which limits disruption. The main costs fall on a small number of chlorine plants, which get a six-year runway to convert. The bill's limits, the trace-impurity exclusion and the grandfathering of installed asbestos, are reasonable transitions but mean it does not address the exposure most Americans actually face today.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, which has not taken it up; no vote has happened and none is scheduled.

narrative.text: Senator Jeff Merkley introduced the bill on September 16, 2025, joined by Senators Blumenthal, Padilla, and Schiff [S1][S3].
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Environment and Public Works the same day [S5].
All three cosponsors are Democrats, and no Republicans have signed on [S4].
The committee has taken no further action on the bill since referral [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, the status quo: chlor-alkali plants may continue importing and using asbestos, and companies selling asbestos-containing products keep their market, since no ban has moved toward a vote.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Industries still using asbestos, for now

sides.party_line_note: All four sponsors are Democrats and no Republican has cosponsored, so early support is entirely one-party, though the bill has not yet come to any vote.

industries.note: These plants are the main U.S. users of chrysotile asbestos, which they import to make chlorine-production diaphragms; the bill ends that use by 2030, forcing conversion to non-asbestos technology. The industry benefits in the short run from the six-year grace period the bill grants to plants already operating.

industries.industry: Asbestos importers and makers of asbestos-containing products
industries.note: The bill bans importing, manufacturing, and selling commercial asbestos and products containing it, cutting off these supply chains. Their products are a source of ongoing worker and consumer exposure, which is what the ban targets.

The bill preserves the market for safely removing and disposing of asbestos already installed in buildings, which is the abatement industry's work. Removal reduces long-term exposure for building occupants.

analysis.trajectory: Most Senate bills die in committee without a vote, and this one has received no action beyond referral, with no Republican cosponsors and a committee led by the opposing party. Its realistic path is to sit in committee unless public attention or a companion House bill changes the calculus.
